snippet:
📝 Here goes another long and perhaps boring investment tweet.

Been tinkering with a few different strategies for a system-driven Tactical Index Portfolio for the US markets using leverage in the form of Leveraged ETFs (LETFs) for the S&P500 and Nasdaq-100 indexes.

None of this is new though, you will find several Reddit and Bogleheads thread exploring ideas along the same lines or a variation of these, most of them stem from the following two papers:

Leverage for the Long Run - A Systematic Approach to Managing Risk and Magnifying Returns in Stocks (2016, Michael Gayed)

Alpha Generation and Risk Smoothing using Managed Volatility (2010, Tony Cooper)

⬆️ Leveraged ETFs

Leverage comes in varying shapes and sizes, most commonly in the Indian markets we have Futures and Options contracts against index and stocks. In the US (and other markets) we also have Leveraged ETFs (LETFs). LETFs provide “easy” access to leverage for non-sophisticated retail investors albeit with a slightly higher fee (expense ratio) than their unlevered counterparts.

For example:

SPY: The vanilla S&P500 index ETF. If you buy $100 of SPY you have $100 of exposure to the S&P500 (SPX).

SSO: A 2x Leveraged SPX ETF. Which means that for every $100 invested into SSO you get $200 of exposure (2x) to the SPX.

From a return point of view, for every 1% rise in SPX, SSO would see a 2% rise (2x). Unsurprisingly, this works on the downside too, so for every 1% of fall in the SPX, SSO would fall by 2%.

title: A simple two-ETF strategy produced a 13.9% compound annual return in the backtest.
snippet:
A simple two-ETF strategy produced a 13.9% compound annual return in the backtest.

The strategy aims to reduce some of the risk of owning a leveraged equity ETF by combining it with long-term US Treasury bonds. 

It uses SSO for leveraged exposure to the S&P 500 and TLT for exposure to long-term Treasury bonds.

The idea is based on the negative correlation between broad equities and long-term Treasury bonds. 

When one side of the portfolio performs strongly, the other may help provide balance during weaker periods.

The entry rule is simple: invest 50% of the portfolio in SSO and 50% in TLT.

There is no traditional exit signal in this version. Instead, the portfolio remains fully invested and is rebalanced once a month. 

Each monthly rebalance restores the original 50/50 allocation by reducing the larger position and adding to the smaller one.

The backtest recorded 400 trades, with an average gain of 1.2% per trade and a 57% win rate. The compound annual return was 13.9%, while the maximum drawdown was 37%.

The result is promising, but the drawdown shows that leverage still carries substantial risk. This is a historical backtest, and future results may be very different.

title: A barbell strategy is an investment approach that balances two extremes: one portion of the portfolio is allocated to lo
snippet:
A barbell strategy is an investment approach that balances two extremes: one portion of the portfolio is allocated to low-risk assets, such as short-term bonds or cash, while the other is invested in high-risk, high-return assets, such as equities, long-term bonds, or speculative investments. The middle-risk segment is deliberately avoided.

Recently, we were approached by an institutional investor seeking to enhance the profitability of a low-duration portfolio, typically invested in short-term U.S. bonds. To address this, we designed a weekly rebalanced portfolio that trades seven highly liquid U.S. futures.

The strategy follows a barbell approach with two distinct components. The low-risk segment applies momentum and short-term reversal signals across the U.S. yield curve and gold, providing stability and defensive characteristics. In contrast, the high-risk segment consists of a dynamically adjusted leveraged exposure to the S&P 500, targeting stable absolute returns while maintaining a clear separation between risk-seeking and defensive allocations.

With a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6.5%, a maximum drawdown (MDD) of approximately 7%, and a Sharpe ratio of 1.15, the portfolio has demonstrated strong risk-adjusted performance over the past 30 years.
